heuristics.rule: Negotiate as a Canadian citizen in terms of mobility leverage when on PGWP
heuristics.condition: When you hold a Post-Graduation Work Permit (open work permit)...
heuristics.action: ...do not concede negotiation leverage based on immigration status; treat yourself as fully mobile
heuristics.because: PGWP is an open work permit — you can work for any employer without employer sponsorship, giving you the same walk-away power as a citizen

heuristics.rule: Never volunteer future LMIA dependency concerns during negotiation
heuristics.condition: When you are a PGWP holder negotiating a first offer or raise...
heuristics.action: ...do not mention concerns about future PR pathways or LMIA needs
heuristics.because: Disclosing future immigration dependency signals to the employer that they have leverage over you, weakening your negotiating position even when that leverage may not actually exist yet

heuristics.rule: Time CEC Express Entry application to achieve PR before PGWP expiry to eliminate LMIA dependency entirely
heuristics.condition: When you have a 3-year PGWP and a NOC TEER 0/1 job offer...
heuristics.action: ...accumulate 12 months of qualifying work, apply for CEC Express Entry, and target PR grant before PGWP expires
heuristics.because: Successfully executing this timeline means you never need an employer-specific LMIA, preserving full negotiation leverage throughout your early Canadian career

heuristics.rule: Use LMIA investment as leverage in raise conversations with current employer, not in new job negotiations
heuristics.condition: When your current employer has already spent $3,000–$6,000+ on LMIA processing for you...
heuristics.action: ...invoke that investment as a data point supporting higher compensation in retention or raise discussions
heuristics.because: The employer's sunk cost in your work authorization is a credible argument for compensation alignment in an existing relationship, but has weak force in attracting a new employer who hasn't yet made that investment

heuristics.rule: Identify GTS-approved employers as competing offer sources to neutralize LMIA timing leverage
heuristics.condition: When your current employer is using LMIA processing time (2–5 months) as implicit leverage to prevent you from leaving...
heuristics.action: ...find a Global Talent Stream-approved competitor who can process LMIA in ~2 weeks, making a competing offer practically viable
heuristics.because: The employer's leverage in this scenario relies entirely on the time-delay moat; GTS approval at a competitor eliminates that moat

heuristics.rule: Delay LMIA disclosure with startups until after receiving an offer
heuristics.condition: When you need LMIA sponsorship and are applying to startup employers...
heuristics.action: ...do not raise the LMIA requirement until you have a formal offer in hand
heuristics.because: Startups are less likely to invest in LMIA processes and will screen you out early if they know upfront; waiting until you have an offer gives you maximum leverage and demonstrated value before the conversation

heuristics.rule: Use specific salary range anchoring with market data sources in Canadian context
heuristics.condition: When making a salary counter-offer in Canada without a competing offer...
heuristics.action: ...cite Glassdoor Canada, Levels.fyi, and Government of Canada Job Bank together to establish a credible market range, then name a specific target number
heuristics.because: Multi-source market data framing signals preparation and makes the number feel externally validated rather than arbitrary

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether you can realistically walk away from an offer or employer, which is the foundation of all negotiation leverage
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether your current or prospective permit is open (PGWP, PR) vs. employer-specific (LMIA-backed, intra-company transfer); open = full leverage, employer-specific = reduced leverage

decision_factors.factor: Time remaining on PGWP relative to CEC eligibility
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If you can achieve PR before PGWP expiry, you never enter LMIA dependency; if you cannot, your negotiation leverage decreases as expiry approaches
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate PGWP expiry date, subtract 12 months of required CEC work experience, subtract ~6 months of Express Entry processing — determine if PR can land before expiry

decision_factors.factor: Whether target or current employer is GTS-approved
decision_factors.why_it_matters: GTS reduces LMIA processing from 2–5 months to ~2 weeks, making competing offers from GTS employers practically usable as leverage rather than theoretical
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check the GTS employer designation list or ask HR directly whether the company has previously used Global Talent Stream

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Large employers are more likely to have existing LMIA processes and legal resources, making them viable competing offer sources for candidates who need sponsorship
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Target Amazon, Google, Microsoft Canada and established scale-ups for competing offers if you need LMIA; avoid relying on startups as LMIA-capable competing offer sources

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Pay transparency and salary history laws differ by province; BC has the Pay Transparency Act prohibiting salary history questions, Ontario does not have equivalent statutory protection
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify which province the role is in; in BC you can cite legal protection if salary history is asked; in Ontario, redirect tactfully without invoking law

decision_factors.factor: Whether employer has already invested in your work authorization
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Prior LMIA investment by a current employer creates a sunk cost argument you can use in raise or retention discussions
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether your current employer paid LMIA fees and legal costs for you; if so, quantify the investment ($3,000–$6,000+) before the conversation

decision_factors.factor: Existence and quality of competing offer
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A real competing offer from an identifiable company is the single strongest negotiation lever regardless of immigration status
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess whether the competing offer is from a named company at a specific dollar amount — vague competing interest has far less force than a specific written offer

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying with LMIA-sponsoring employer past PGWP expiry without achieving PR
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You become employer-tied at the exact moment your career leverage should be increasing; your job market effectively shrinks to only LMIA-capable employers, and your ability to walk away from a bad compensation situation disappears
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PGWP holders who delay CEC Express Entry applications or who fail to accumulate NOC TEER 0/1 experience quickly enough

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Disclosing LMIA need early in the application process to startups
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Screening occurs before you can demonstrate value; you lose the chance to convert genuine interest into an offer that creates negotiation context
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who need LMIA and are applying to early-stage or growth-stage companies without established immigration infrastructure

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating weakly on first Canadian job offer as PGWP holder due to assumed future LMIA dependency
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If you execute the clean PGWP → CEC → PR timeline, you had full mobility the entire time and left money on the table unnecessarily; the assumed leverage the employer had was never real
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who understand immigration at a surface level but don't map their specific timeline against PR eligibility thresholds

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using employer LMIA investment argument in a new job negotiation (rather than a retention context)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The argument lacks credibility because the new employer has no sunk cost — it can come across as trying to import a relationship asset that doesn't exist yet, weakening rather than strengthening the ask
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who successfully used the LMIA investment argument internally and attempt to replicate it in external offer negotiations

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a bridging open work permit without verifying whether it remains tied to original employer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A bridging open work permit tied to the original employer provides the appearance of mobility without the reality; leaving the employer may void work authorization even though the permit says 'open'
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in late-stage PR application processes who believe they have full mobility because their permit says 'open'

failure_patterns.pattern: PGWP holders negotiating as if they are employer-tied when they are not
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Conflation of the Canadian immigration system with the US H-1B model; students assume any work authorization creates employer leverage because that's the dominant narrative in international student communities
failure_patterns.consequence: Accepting below-market offers or failing to counter at all during the period of maximum mobility leverage — typically the first 1–2 years of Canadian employment
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I don't want to push too hard because I might need them for my PR'
Candidate has not researched their PGWP expiry date versus CEC eligibility timeline

failure_patterns.pattern: Delaying CEC Express Entry application until late in PGWP validity period
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Focus on job performance and unfamiliarity with immigration timelines; candidates assume there is more buffer than exists once processing times are factored in
failure_patterns.consequence: PR not granted before PGWP expiry, triggering actual employer dependency and LMIA need — turning an assumed weakness into a real one
warning_signs: Candidate is 18+ months into PGWP with NOC TEER 0/1 experience but has not started Express Entry profile
Candidate is unaware of current Express Entry processing times or CEC draw frequency

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating all competing offers as equally usable leverage regardless of LMIA logistics
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates focus on the dollar value of a competing offer without assessing whether the competing employer can actually complete the work authorization transfer in a practical timeframe
failure_patterns.consequence: Competing offer leverage collapses when the current employer correctly points out that the competing offer requires a 3–5 month LMIA process — the bluff is called
warning_signs: Competing offer is from a company with no prior LMIA history and no GTS designation
Candidate has not verified LMIA processing pathway before using the offer in negotiation

failure_patterns.pattern: Answering 'Do you need sponsorship?' as 'Yes' when on PGWP
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates conflate long-term PR sponsorship needs with current work authorization requirements; they interpret the question as asking about their eventual immigration trajectory rather than their current legal work status
failure_patterns.consequence: Screened out of roles where they were fully eligible to work immediately, losing interview opportunities unnecessarily
warning_signs: Candidate does not have a prepared, accurate one-sentence description of their current work permit status
Candidate has checked 'Yes' to sponsorship questions on job applications while holding an active PGWP

failure_patterns.pattern: Raising LMIA requirement with startups before receiving an offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Desire to avoid wasted effort or perceived transparency obligation; candidates disclose immigration needs in cover letters or early screening calls
failure_patterns.consequence: Screened out before demonstrating value; foregoes any chance of converting genuine technical interest into an offer that could then be negotiated
warning_signs: Candidate mentions visa status in cover letter or application form to companies without established immigration programs
Candidate asks about sponsorship policy in the first recruiter screen before receiving any signal of interest

diagnostic_questions.question: What specific type of work permit do you currently hold — is it open or employer-specific?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines the actual level of negotiation leverage available; this is the single most important variable before any other advice is relevant
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If open (PGWP): What is your PGWP expiry date, and have you calculated whether you can achieve PR before that date?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If employer-specific: Who is the employer named on the permit, and have you identified any GTS-approved alternative employers you could approach for competing offers?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you accumulated 12 months of NOC TEER 0/1 Canadian work experience?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether you are currently eligible to apply for CEC Express Entry, which is the mechanism for eliminating LMIA dependency
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you created an Express Entry profile and received an ITA? If not, this is the most urgent action to restore or preserve negotiation leverage.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: How many months remain until you reach 12 months, and does that timeline fit within your PGWP validity with sufficient buffer for PR processing?

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the employer you are negotiating with (or any competing employer you are considering) appear on the Global Talent Stream designation list?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether competing offers are practically usable as leverage (GTS = ~2 weeks) or theoretically usable but practically slow (standard LMIA = 2–5 months)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: GTS-approved competing employers give you real walk-away power even without open work authorization; use competing offer leverage normally.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The competing offer may not be credible as a lever if the LMIA timeline makes it impractical; assess whether to disclose it or seek a GTS-approved alternative first

diagnostic_questions.question: Has your current employer already paid for LMIA processing and legal fees on your behalf?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the employer investment argument is available in a raise or retention conversation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Quantify the investment ($3,000–$6,000+) and determine whether it has been raised in prior compensation conversations; if not, it is a credible new data point for a raise ask.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The investment argument is unavailable; focus compensation conversation on market data and delivered contributions instead

diagnostic_questions.question: In which province is the role located — specifically, is it BC or Ontario?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines which legal framework applies to salary history questions and pay transparency obligations
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If BC: You are protected by the Pay Transparency Act and can explicitly decline to answer salary history questions by citing the law.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Ontario or other provinces: Redirect salary history questions tactfully without citing statutory protection, as the legal basis is weaker

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a specific competing offer from a named company at a specific dollar figure, or only general market interest?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Distinguishes between leverage that will survive employer scrutiny and leverage that will collapse under a basic follow-up question
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Verify the competing employer's LMIA or GTS status before deploying the offer as leverage to ensure it is practically actionable, not just nominally attractive.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Without a specific competing offer, shift to market data anchoring strategy using Glassdoor Canada, Levels.fyi, and Government of Canada Job Bank rather than competing offer framing

industry_realities.common_belief: International students in Canada always need employer sponsorship and therefore have reduced negotiation power
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP holders have an open work permit giving them identical mobility to Canadian citizens during the permit's validity — there is no employer-tied immigration dependency unless the candidate allows themselves to approach expiry without PR
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders should negotiate with full leverage from day one, treating immigration status as irrelevant to the negotiation rather than as a concession they must make

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian employers face the same LMIA burden as US employers face with H-1B, creating equivalent premium justification
industry_realities.actual_reality: Unlike H-1B, LMIA in Canada does not create ongoing employer lock-in for most international students who will transition through CEC Express Entry; the retention leverage argument is much weaker in Canada
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not expect LMIA costs to generate automatic salary premiums in new job negotiations; the argument has force only in existing employer retention conversations

industry_realities.common_belief: Any LMIA-backed competing offer provides usable negotiation leverage
industry_realities.actual_reality: A competing offer requiring 2–5 months of standard LMIA processing is practically unusable as immediate leverage; employers know this and will not feel threatened by an offer you cannot realistically take for months
industry_realities.implication: Candidates needing LMIA sponsorship should specifically target GTS-approved employers for competing offers, since only these create practically credible walk-away alternatives

industry_realities.common_belief: Checking 'Yes' to the sponsorship question on Canadian job applications is required honesty for PGWP holders
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP is an open work permit; the accurate and legally correct answer is that no LMIA or employer sponsorship is required for current work authorization
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders should answer sponsorship questions as 'No' or clarify 'I hold an open work permit and do not require employer-specific sponsorship,' avoiding unnecessary screening-out from roles they are legally eligible to take immediately

industry_realities.common_belief: Bridging open work permits provide the same mobility as a PGWP
industry_realities.actual_reality: Some bridging open work permits are tied to the original sponsoring employer; leaving that employer may invalidate work authorization even if the permit category sounds open
industry_realities.implication: Candidates in PR application processes should verify the specific conditions of their bridging permit before assuming they have the same walk-away leverage as PGWP holders

industry_realities.common_belief: 'Sponsorship' means the same thing to all Canadian employers asking the question
industry_realities.actual_reality: The question is ambiguous in Canada — it may mean LMIA specifically, or any work permit assistance at all; the interpretation varies by employer and HR sophistication
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should proactively clarify their current status ('I hold an open work permit') rather than answering a binary yes/no, which avoids both dishonesty and unnecessary self-disqualification

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes immigration status automatically disadvantages them in negotiation; conflates Canadian PGWP with US H-1B employer-tied dynamics without examining the actual portability of their specific permit
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Maps their specific permit type against actual employer dependency; recognizes that PGWP = full mobility and plans the CEC timeline proactively to ensure that mobility is preserved through the PR transition
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A junior who negotiates as if constrained when they are not leaves real money on the table during the highest-mobility window of their Canadian career

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Competing offer construction for LMIA-dependent candidates
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Sources any competing offer at a higher dollar figure and presents it as leverage, without verifying whether the competing employer can actually complete work authorization transfer in a practical timeframe
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Specifically targets GTS-approved employers for competing offers, ensuring the competing offer is practically executable (2-week LMIA) rather than theoretically attractive but logistically impractical
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A competing offer that collapses under basic scrutiny about LMIA timelines destroys credibility and weakens the negotiation more than having no competing offer at all

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Timing of LMIA disclosure with startups
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Discloses LMIA need early out of a sense of fairness or to avoid wasted effort, effectively self-screening before the employer has assessed their value
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Withholds LMIA disclosure until an offer is received, allowing demonstrated value and genuine employer interest to create the conditions for a productive LMIA conversation
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: An employer who has already decided they want to hire you will solve immigration logistics; an employer who hasn't yet will treat LMIA as a reason to choose a simpler candidate

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Answers 'Yes' to sponsorship questions while on PGWP because they're thinking about future PR needs rather than current legal work authorization status
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Answers with a precise description of current permit status: 'I hold an open work permit and do not require employer-specific sponsorship' — accurate, non-self-disqualifying, and invites no follow-up concern
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Incorrect 'Yes' answers to sponsorship questions cause candidates to be screened out of roles they were legally eligible for, eliminating interview opportunities that would have generated competing offer leverage

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Strategic use of LMIA investment argument
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Uses the employer's LMIA investment as an argument when negotiating with a new employer (who has made no such investment), expecting it to generate sympathy or premium
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Reserves the LMIA investment argument exclusively for retention or raise conversations with the current employer who actually made the investment, where the sunk cost argument is credible
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Misapplied, the argument reads as irrelevant or entitled to a new employer; correctly applied, it adds a legitimate data point to a raise conversation that the employer cannot easily dismiss

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Immigration timeline planning as career strategy
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats immigration milestones (PGWP, PR application) as administrative tasks to handle reactively when they become urgent
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Proactively calculates the full PGWP → CEC → PR timeline at the start of employment, ensuring negotiation leverage is preserved by design rather than luck
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Candidates who fail to plan this timeline may find themselves in LMIA dependency precisely when they are most experienced and most capable of extracting maximum compensation — they trade away leverage at the worst possible time
